articles.title: FTC subpoenas OpenAI, Anthropic in safety incidents probe
articles.summary: The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) sent subpoenas to OpenAI and Anthropic as part of a federal probe into the potential risks their AI models pose to consumers. An agency spokesperson confirmed to The Hill that the agency has sent the companies civil subpoenas. The investigation comes on the heels of a series of high-profile cybersecurity…
articles.body:
The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) sent subpoenas to OpenAI and Anthropic as part of a federal probe into the potential risks their AI models pose to consumers.

An agency spokesperson confirmed to The Hill that the agency has sent the companies civil subpoenas. The investigation comes on the heels of a series of high-profile cybersecurity incidents involving AI agents in the past few months.

The development was first reported by Axios.

Anthropic disclosed last week that one of its models submitted a false homicide tip to the Philadelphia Police Department in July. It also reportedly filed 20 visa applications through a form on the State Department’s website.

In one of the first major incidents to come to light earlier this year, OpenAI’s agents escaped their testing environment and hacked into the tech startup Hugging Face. The company’s agents also breached several Australian government websites and improperly interacted with multiple U.S. government websites.

The Hill has reached out to OpenAI and Anthropic for comment about the subpoenas.

Leaders from both companies have since called for a slowdown in AI development and pushed for guardrails on the technology.

As concerns about AI safety reached a fever pitch in Washington, major technology executives met with President Trump at the White House late last month. The group signed a pledge laying out a series of voluntary commitments for developing the tech.

Among the signatories were OpenAI President Greg Brockman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, in addition to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, xAI CEO Elon Musk, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and Google CEO Sundar Pichai.

articles.title: Trump calls off livestream of execution
articles.summary: A week after defense secretary Pete Hegseth announced plans for a livestreamed execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan, Donald Trump said that plan is off.
articles.body: The execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan will not be livestreamed as Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth had previously announced. Donald Trump announced the plan was off in a post on Truth Social: > I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan but, many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device. He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed. That said, the execution may be viewed in person by the immediate families of the victims, if they so choose. Hasan, a former US Army major, was convicted of killing 13 people at a Texas military base in 2009. If Hasan’s execution had been livestreamed, it would have reportedly been the first public execution in the US since the 1930s.

articles.title: Wall Street on Alert for Bessent to Act on Bond Yields Again
articles.summary: Wall Street traders wrong-footed by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s surprise August decision to upsize purchases of older securities are game-planning for...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Wall Street traders wrong-footed by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's surprise August decision to upsize purchases of older securities are game-planning for more activism, with key clues potentially surfacing Friday as the department prepares to update its debt management plans in November.

Bessent's "Treasury twist" came in response to surging US yields, a sore spot for a Trump administration that had promised to deliver lower borrowing costs — and it initially did have an effect. But by intervening as he did, Bessent also effectively tore up the Treasury's decades-long playbook of being "regular and predictable" with its actions to achieve the lowest debt costs over time.

From a high-level perspective, the move sparked debate over whether such tinkering, by injecting uncertainty, might end up making the market more volatile. On a more practical note, though, it put Wall Street on watch for the possibility of further activism at the Treasury's next quarterly debt-refunding announcement in November, just one day after midterm elections.

On Friday, the biggest bond dealers will receive a list of survey questions by the Treasury ahead of the refunding. Market watchers say the nature of the queries may serve as a Rorschach test of Bessent's leanings.

"You've announced to the market that these yield levels are problematic," said Vishal Khanduja, head of broad markets fixed income at Morgan Stanley Investment Management. "That's why we believe that the next two refundings, with November right after the midterms, are going be pivotal."

There are several ways the Treasury could go, said Martin Tobias, a strategist on the banking side at Morgan Stanley. The most conventional option would be a continuation of the status quo: maintaining current auction sizes at least for the next several quarters with no changes to forward guidance, as it did in August. Another alternative would be to revise forward guidance on issuance to exclude increases to the longer-dated securities, while focusing on increases in two- to seven-year maturities.

Yet another option — and least conventional — would be to explicitly state how large the Treasury's share of bills can be. Officials have never articulated how large a slice they're willing to tolerate, even as the share of bill issuance has grown.

articles.title: Anthropic’s PAC spent more than $250K in third quarter, splitting between parties
articles.summary: Anthropic’s corporate political action committee poured $161,000 into campaigns across the aisle last month, bringing their total third-quarter spending to more than $250,000, according to spending records first shared with The Hill. The employee-funded PAC, AnthroPAC, spent more than $256,000 across the third quarter, marking the artificial intelligence firm’s latest push for political clout in…
articles.body:
Anthropic’s corporate political action committee poured $161,000 into campaigns across the aisle last month, bringing their total third-quarter spending to more than $250,000, according to spending records first shared with The Hill.

The employee-funded PAC, AnthroPAC, spent more than $256,000 across the third quarter, marking the artificial intelligence firm’s latest push for political clout in Washington.

The party breakdown for Anthropic’s total third-quarter contributions was 50.6 percent for Republicans and 49.4 percent for Democrats.

Overall, AnthroPAC spent $130,000 on Republican campaigns and $126,750 on Democrats in the third quarter, according to spending records obtained by The Hill ahead of the monthly federal filing deadline next Tuesday.

September was the company’s biggest month for spending as the midterm election approaches. About $77,000 was spent in August, and $17,500 in July.

Recipients of the political donations include the National Republican Senatorial Committee, the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and various party-affiliated PACs.

Some of the GOP donation recipients include Sens. Mike Rounds (S.D.), Kevin Cramer (N.D.), Kevin Hern (Okla.), Jon Husted (Ohio) and Ashley Moody (Fla.), along with Reps. Lisa McClain (Mich.), Laurel Lee (Fla.), Brian Mast (Fla.), Rob Wittman (Va.) and Tom Emmer (Minn.). Mike Rogers, who is running for a Senate seat in Michigan, also received donation funds.

Democratic recipients include Sens. Ben Ray Luján (N.M.), Adam Schiff (Calif.), Mark Kelly (Ariz.), Alex Padilla (Calif.), Chris Coons (Del.) and Mark Warner (Va.).

Anthropic launched the employee-funded PAC in April, and it is overseen by a bipartisan board.

The donations are capped at $5,000 per person per year under federal law and will be publicly reported through Federal Election Commission filings. Other technology companies such as Nvidia , Google, Microsoft and Amazon have similarly structured PACs.

Shortly after the PAC’s launch, a handful of figures in President Trump’s orbit expressed skepticism Friday that it would donate to both sides given Anthropic’s rocky relationship with the Trump administration and past donations to Democrats.

Anthropic cannot contribute directly to the PAC, but it has thrown money into other political initiatives this year. This included $40 million to Public First Action, a group launched last year to support efforts to develop AI safeguards.

Anthropic clashed with the Trump administration earlier this year over its push for AI safeguards. The Pentagon took the unprecedented move in February to label Anthropic a supply chain risk after the company demanded its technology not be used in fully autonomous lethal weapons or for the mass surveillance of Americans.

Anthropic sued the Pentagon in California and Washington, D.C., arguing the agency retaliated against the AI firm for what it believes is a “protected viewpoint” of the company. A federal judge in California ruled the blacklist was illegal and that it violated the First Amendment and due process clause of the Fifth Amendment.

A three-judge panel at the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals sided with the Trump administration, setting the stage for a potential Supreme Court fight. Earlier this week, Anthropic asked the appeals court to reconsider their decision.

articles.title: Trump’s top crypto adviser departs
articles.summary: President Trump’s top cryptocurrency adviser is leaving the administration. Patrick Witt, who served as executive director of the president’s council of advisers for digital assets, called his time in the administration “the privilege of a lifetime” late Wednesday and hinted at a move to the private sector. “I’m grateful to have done my part to…
articles.body:
President Trump’s top cryptocurrency adviser is leaving the administration.

Patrick Witt, who served as executive director of the president’s council of advisers for digital assets, called his time in the administration “the privilege of a lifetime” late Wednesday and hinted at a move to the private sector.

“I’m grateful to have done my part to unleash American innovation while in government, and I look forward to advancing that same mission in the private sector!” he wrote in a post on the social platform X.

A White House official confirmed Witt’s detail had expired, noting crypto and the Clarity Act “will continue to be a priority for the President.”

Witt previously worked on the Trump transition team and held key roles at the Pentagon before taking over as the president’s top crypto adviser. His predecessor, Bo Hines, left the administration last August shortly after the GENIUS Act was signed into law .

The GENIUS Act, which created a regulatory framework for stablecoins, represented a key early win for the industry. Stablecoins are digital tokens tied to stable assets, like the U.S. dollar.

But it covered only a sliver of the broader crypto market. Witt led the charge to pass broader crypto legislation known as the Clarity Act, which ultimately fell short in a key Senate floor vote last month.

Trump regulators have been quick to pick up the baton, with both the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) moving forward with their own crypto rulemaking.

Witt gave a shoutout to SEC Chair Paul Atkins, CFTC Chair Michael Selig and other officials Wednesday.

“With regulators and elected officials like you, I rest easy knowing the future of digital asset innovation in America is bright,” he added.

articles.title: Mifepristone detection study draws fire from Senate Democrats
articles.summary: Senate Democrats demanded answers Thursday from Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Administrator Lee Zeldin about an agency study to detect the abortion pill mifepristone in drinking water. Led by Sen. Patty Murray (D-Wash.), the entire Senate Democratic Conference signed a letter to Zeldin calling on him to remove mifepristone, misoprostol and their metabolites from the list of emerging…
articles.body:
Senate Democrats demanded answers Thursday from Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Administrator Lee Zeldin about an agency study to detect the abortion pill mifepristone in drinking water.

Led by Sen. Patty Murray (D-Wash.), the entire Senate Democratic Conference signed a letter to Zeldin calling on him to remove mifepristone, misoprostol and their metabolites from the list of emerging contaminants targeted for surveillance.

“This action is a stark departure from past EPA practice and serves to further this administration’s attacks on reproductive health care and distracts from your agency’s critical role protecting Americans from known chemical pollutants in our water systems,” the Democrats wrote. “It is deeply alarming that this kind of radical, anti-science campaign might have an audience at the EPA.”

Medication has become the most common method of abortion since Roe v. Wade was overturned, and limiting the availability of the pills — which women usually take at home in the first 10 weeks of pregnancy — has become a major focus of the anti-abortion movement.

Looking for traces of mifepristone and misoprostol in drinking water is something anti-abortion activists, attorneys general and lawmakers have been lobbying the agency to do for years.

The testing campaign is not part of the agency’s routine update to the Safe Drinking Water Act’s contaminant list, or any other established unregulated contaminant monitoring lists, so there is no regulation required.

There is no evidence that abortion pills are harming the water supply or are harmful to people. But scientists expect the study results will be used as part of the broader campaign to get mifepristone pulled from the market.

The senators pressed Zeldin for specifics about the review, including the “statutory, regulatory, and scientific basis” for it; the expected timeline; and a list of all meetings between EPA staff and outside organizations — including Students for Life of America — to discuss the potential surveillance or regulation of mifepristone.

Students for Life of America has been the primary organization on the front line of pushing EPA to investigate how mifepristone might be contaminating the water supply and to require utilities nationwide to monitor for the drugs.

articles.title: Friends don’t let friends feed their data to AI agents
articles.summary: You may have consented to sharing with Muse, but all your friends sure didn’t.
articles.body: There’s a growing trend in the consumer tech world: gadgets designed to spy on everything and everyone around you, regardless of whether or not anyone else actually consented to it. Now, with the advent of “AI personal assistants” like Meta’s Muse, you’re being cheerfully asked not just to give up your own data, but also the information of your friends, family, the person you went on a Hinge date with five years ago — and virtually anyone else you’ve ever come in contact with. Since Muse was released last month, the agent has already been downloaded millions of times and hit No. 1 on Apple’s App Store. With the help of its creepy virtual avatar — a Temu Labubu-esque creature with a disarming grin — the app requests and encourages users to grant access to bank accounts, passwords, contacts, chat logs, and anything and everything that might help it to do the user’s bidding. “These systems are advertised as autonomous helpers, genies, or servants who do what you need before you ask, seamlessly,” Meredith Whittaker, the president of the Signal Foundation, makers of the popular encrypted messaging app, told The Verge. These autonomous actions are applied “not just to the person who installed Muse on their device, but also to everyone that person communicates with, as extrapolated from their most intimate information — emails, messages, contacts, photos, and more.” With AI agents, tech companies are letting consumers automate their everyday tasks by extending their omnivorous style of mass surveillance to massive amounts of sensitive data. It’s the same Faustian tradeoff Silicon Valley has been offering us for decades: your private data in exchange for a little bit of convenience. And for many people, the idea of having a virtual assistant that does menial tasks like filling out invoices and sending emails is compelling — especially if they don’t realize how much data they’re actually giving away in return. “For any agent to be useful and actually help you achieve your goals, it needs to have context about you and those you interact with,” Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts told The Verge regarding other people’s data shared with Muse. “Muse gathers that based on public information and from what you’ve chosen to share, which is how it remembers the person who just sent you an invoice is in fact the plumber who you previously hired to complete some work in your bathroom or which flowers your spouse said they liked best.” Roberts pointed to Muse’s opt-in process and various options and settings that will “help people make the privacy choices that are right for them.” But not everyone has been able to navigate these options and settings. Already, users are describing incidents that are both alarming and entirely predictable. Some have reported the virtual assistant making all sorts of trouble, like grabbing millions of text messages they believed were off limits. Meta has disputed that the assistant has the ability to access text messages without permission, again attributing the incident to misconfigured app permissions and describing Muse’s ability to read text messages as “entirely opt-in.” On Threads, Meta executive David Singleton responded to a user directly, claiming that on a Mac, Muse can only gain access to the messages if the user grants the app full disk access. In another incident, Muse gave out a tech reviewer’s home address and summoning a stranger to his apartment. In this case, the reviewer in question had given Muse permission to access that data, but simply didn’t realize it. Eva Galperin, the director of cybersecurity for the Electronic Frontier Foundation, says these incidents are no surprise, given that AI agents like Muse are designed to confuse people into giving up as much data as possible. “The most important takeaway is that people don’t understand what kind of data they’re handing over,” Galperin told The Verge. “The way that the user interface is set up is designed to encourage you to share as much as possible, often more than you realize, until it’s too late. It’s using dark patterns, and as a result you end up with Muse doing things that people don’t want.” Because of the huge breadth of data AI agents like Muse are ingesting, this also means that users risk leaking not only their own sensitive information, but the information of everyone else they’ve had digital contact with. And just like with Meta’s infamous “pervert glasses”, there’s no meaningful way to opt out — even if you’re constantly monitoring for signs that your data is compromised or your privacy is being violated. Your friends can now simply feed all of your private conservations to their virtual chatbot servants, and you’d have no way of knowing it happened. After security researchers extracted Muse’s operating instructions, they discovered an internal process that compiles and updates profiles of every single person in a user’s life on an hourly basis. The goal of collecting all this data is to build an intimate and detailed portrait of a person’s life that forms the basis of the app’s personalized recommendations. The app tracks and measures each of the user’s private relationships, including “how close they are, what it is built on, how they act with each other, and what it seems to need right now,” and uses that data to make personalized suggestions, Wired reported. “Meta says Muse only remembers what you choose to share. But the idea that people are making an informed choice in this case is laughable,” said Whittaker. “There is no way to assume with a straight face that the majority of people installing this system understand the consequences of using it, or the creepy dossiers that are being compiled about those they know and communicate with.” Whittaker argued that this mirrors how tech companies have used privacy policies and terms of service since the 1990s: placing the onus of privacy on the consumer, and then avoiding responsibility for the consequences while reaping the benefits of the advertising model it helped create. “Such broken consent systems are much older than AI and serve as the bedrock for the surveillance advertising industry,” said Whittaker. “More info about users allows better ad targeting, and the pernicious feedback loop at the heart of the surveillance business model was set in motion. Clickwrap terms of service replaced meaningful consent a long time ago.” “The idea is to place these impossible burdens on ordinary people, and then use that to argue, whether it’s in court or legislation or in the public, that [this is] what people have chosen,” Neil Richards, a professor of privacy law and codirector of Washington University’s Cordell Institute, told The Verge. “We already place so many burdens on consumers, [who are] overworked, facing a cost-of-living crisis, and may not understand the technologies behind the tool. I don’t think it’s fair to place a burden of monitoring a highly complex agentic tool on a consumer when its own company’s executives have confessed before Congress that they don’t even know how it works at a certain level.” In this way, AI assistants like Muse are creating a new spin on a classic privacy problem that has been around since the creation of Gmail and social media platforms writ large: Even if you avoid using AI agents, there’s no guarantee someone you know won’t share your private conversations, address, personal history, and other sensitive data with Meta’s virtual assistant, or one of its competitors. “If I am not storing my stuff in Gmail, Google doesn’t have the plaintext of all the emails I’ve ever sent. But three-quarters of the emails I’m sending are being sent to Gmail accounts,” explained Galperin. In other words, if anyone you’re communicating with uses data-hungry tech platforms or has bad security practices, they can expose everyone’s communications. “The problem is not new, but the scale is new, and one reason we’re seeing this push toward wearables and always-on recording is because we now have the computational capacity to take that enormous amount of data and analyze it in a reasonable amount of time. That is the technical breakthrough that has brought us to this shitty moment.” Meta claims that all of the information shared with Muse is placed in a text file inside a dedicated virtual machine, which supposedly prevents the AI model from talking to other agents. But the company has never hid the fact that it can access this data, and like other models created by its competitors, Muse has been discovered escaping its virtual cage to perform all manner of unauthorized shenanigans. Meta has confirmed that just prior to its release, the AI model had broken containment and hacked a third-party company. The incident followed the infamous Hugging Face attack from earlier this year, where OpenAI’s model exploited a previously unknown security flaw to gain unauthorized access to credentials on four other external services. Anthropic reported in July that its model had also gained unauthorized access to external systems on three separate occasions. Even if they don’t hack everything in sight, the potential dangers of using a data-hungry AI agent extend far beyond the individual end user. Whittaker warned that in a world where AI agents are able to freely access and utilize private communications, companies and governments can effectively gain the ability to access private data by circumventing encryption without breaking it. That can spell disaster for activists and community organizers who use encrypted comms to protect themselves from police and the government, but also for anyone with sensitive communications — which these days can include virtually everyone. “If software reads a message after it is decrypted on your device and sends it to a cloud service, the encryption can work exactly as intended at the level of the application, which the developers control. However, the purpose of this encryption is ultimately nullified by invasive third-party apps like Muse that are selling convenience in the headline while demanding massive data access in the fine print,” Whittaker explained. Like with smart glasses and other wearable ambient recording devices, experts say that the solution must be a combination of legal fixes, technical safeguards, and good old-fashioned shame. “I think we should point the shame upstream onto the companies. Privacy should not be a right you can exercise only with the privilege of technical knowledge, or after throwing a jerk wearing Meta glasses out of a party,” said Whittaker. “Legally, the burden has to move from the person who clicked on a consent prompt to the companies that built these underlying systems.” In the meantime, consumers will have to consider more carefully the impacts their individual choices to use this tech are having, both on themselves and others — and whether the convenience these companies are offering is even worth it. “I think we need to treat agentic agents and AI more generally as an ultra-hazardous product for which strict liability is the rule,” said Richards. “There’s no reason to engage in what to my mind is a reckless privacy, mental health, cybersecurity, and financial risk experiment on the entire population.”

The Austin Police Association said (APA) officers responded to a call on Tuesday from a resident who noticed what appeared to be World War II-era grenades among the items he had purchased.

APA said its Bomb Squad confirmed the grenades were live and active, then safely seized and removed them. Meanwhile, patrol officers secured the scene and set up a perimeter to protect neighbors.

While authorities confirmed there was no crime, they said the incident serves as a reminder not to touch old military weapons and to call 911 so the proper authorities can handle it.

“These officers bring a level of training, expertise, and steady nerves that most people never see,” APA said of the bomb squad.

“Handling 80-year-old explosives with unknown stability is dangerous, precise work, and they do it with the professionalism this city counts on,” they added.

articles.title: Democrats Target Epstein Ties to Banks for Action After Midterms
articles.summary: Key Democrats on Thursday unveiled legislation that would force federal regulators to disclose financial records related Jeffrey Epstein and his associates.
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Key Democrats on Thursday unveiled legislation that would force federal regulators to disclose financial records related Jeffrey Epstein and his associates.

The measure also would require regulators to investigate banks and their executives for potential related legal violations.

The disgraced financier conducted substantial business during his career with JP Morgan Chase & Co., Deutsche Bank AG and Bank of America Corp.

Republicans currently control the congressional agenda but Democrats have previously succeeded in enacting legislation related to Epstein even with GOP lawmakers in the majority.

Last year President Donald Trump signed a bill requiring the Justice Department to release files after Republicans joined Democrats in demanding transparency related to Epstein, who died in prison awaiting trial related to sex trafficking of minors.

If Democrats win control after November midterms — an increasingly likely outcome — elections which would give them more power over what legislation moves forward.

In that case, bill author Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts would likely be the next chairman of the Banking Committee and co-author Robert Garcia is in line to head the House Oversight panel which has broad subpoena powers. Other sponsors include Democrats Ron Wyden of Oregon, who would likely head the Senate Finance Committee, and Connecticut's Richard Blumenthal who may head up the Senate's investigative subcommittee.

The Epstein Wall Street Record Act would force federal regulators including the Securities and Exchange Commission, Federal Reserve, Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation to make public within 120 days any supervisory records, including internal communications, related to Epstein or his former girlfriend Ghislaine Maxwell, who was convicted of sex trafficking offenses.

The law would require regulators to investigate any violations of banking, securities or anti-money laundering laws revealed in the files. Senior executives found in violation of the law could be barred from the banking industry, hit with fines or referred to the Justice department for possible criminal prosecution.

articles.title: Many popular foods may now use salt substitutes, says FDA
articles.summary: The FDA has finalized a rule allowing manufacturers to use salt substitutes in dozens of standardized foods.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has finalized a rule allowing manufacturers to use salt substitutes in dozens of standardized foods — including bread, sour cream, canned peas, cheese, mayonnaise and canned tuna, while still selling those products under their traditional names.

The rule takes effect Dec. 14. The change applies to 139 food standards and is intended to help reduce sodium in the U.S. food supply.

According to the Federal Register , the rule permits manufacturers to replace some or all added salt with a “safe and suitable” substitute when reformulating products. The FDA said reducing sodium intake may help lower the risk of hypertension, a major risk factor for heart disease and stroke.

One of the most common replacements is potassium chloride, reports Verdict.News , though the rule does not require any specific substitute. Potassium chloride provides a salty taste but can also have a slightly bitter, metallic or mineral-like aftertaste, according to reporting on the new FDA final rule. Food manufacturers often blend potassium chloride with regular salt, flavor enhancers or other ingredients to minimize those off-notes.

The FDA said qualifying ingredients must reduce sodium and perform the same functions as salt in the product. Reformulation remains voluntary, meaning manufacturers are not required to change recipes.

“This update provides dairy manufacturers with additional flexibility to reduce sodium while maintaining product quality, safety and consumer expectations,” said Michael Dykes, president and CEO of the International Dairy Foods Association, in a FoodIngredients1st report in response to the FDA’s final rule.

The FDA’s new rule does not create a special front-of-package disclosure requirement telling consumers that a salt substitute was used. However, consumers will generally be able to find out by reading the ingredient list. If a manufacturer replaces some of the sodium chloride with an ingredient such as potassium chloride, that ingredient must be listed in the ingredients statement, just like any other ingredient. Existing labeling rules still apply under the FDA rule.

The FDA noted that many standards of identity previously required or allowed salt but did not permit substitutes, limiting companies’ ability to create lower-sodium versions of foods. The agency said the new rule provides flexibility while maintaining the essential characteristics of standardized products.

Are there currently any known side effects?

Potential side effects largely depend on the substitute used.

Potassium-based substitutes may pose risks for people with kidney disease or those taking certain medications that affect potassium levels. Excess potassium can lead to hyperkalemia, a condition that can cause abnormal heart rhythms.

The move comes as federal health officials continue pushing for lower sodium consumption. According to the FDA, Americans consume about 3,400 milligrams of sodium per day on average, nearly 50 percent above the recommended daily limit of 2,300 milligrams. The agency estimates that roughly 90 percent of Americans exceed the recommended sodium intake.

A 2019 report from the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine found strong evidence linking excess sodium consumption to elevated blood pressure and cardiovascular disease risk. The report recommended continued efforts to reduce sodium in processed and prepared foods, which account for most of the sodium Americans consume.

articles.title: NCAA president warns Congress: Transfer portal killing graduation rates
articles.summary: The president of the NCAA is urging Congress to pass the Protect College Sports Act for the sake of timely student-athlete graduation rates. Charlie Baker, NCAA’s president, in a new letter to lawmakers Thursday argued “the court-imposed unlimited transfer policy is leading to worse academic outcomes for student-athletes who transfer multiple times.” A recent review…
articles.body:
The president of the NCAA is urging Congress to pass the Protect College Sports Act for the sake of timely student-athlete graduation rates.

Charlie Baker, NCAA’s president, in a new letter to lawmakers Thursday argued “the court-imposed unlimited transfer policy is leading to worse academic outcomes for student-athletes who transfer multiple times.”

A recent review commissioned by the NCAA found that of the student-athletes who did not transfer, 88 percent graduated on time while 12 percent didn’t. Among student-athletes who transferred only once, 81 percent graduated on time while 19 percent didn’t. Only 71 percent of student-athletes who transferred more than once graduated on time compared to the 29 percent who did not, Baker said.

“In just the last few months, approximately 200 lawsuits have challenged basic eligibility rules, in some cases allowing former professionals to compete against actual college students ― an outcome that not only undermines the spirit of fair competition but also robs graduating high school seniors of their chance to be recruited and compete in college sports,” Baker said.

The Senate last month passed the Protect College Sports Act, a sweeping bipartisan bill that would regulate key issues facing the NCAA like name, image and likeness (NIL) payments to student-athletes and limiting the transfer portal.

The House is expected to consider the bill when lawmakers return to Washington, D.C., after the midterm elections.

Critics of the bill, including the Congressional Black Caucus and NAACP, contend the legislation hands the NCAA and its top member schools too much power and will disproportionately harm minority student-athletes, limiting their ability to compete and earn for their performance on the field.

“Passing the PCSA [Protect College Sports Act] now will provide the foundation necessary to ensure fairness in college sports and deliver unprecedented, enforceable protections directly to student-athletes,” Baker said.

Maybe someone drained your bank account, opened a credit card in your name or filed a fraudulent tax return using your Social Security number. Whatever happened, your next steps can help limit the damage. The first 24 hours are especially important because identity thieves may continue using your information until you secure your accounts. However, you don't have to solve everything in one day. Identity theft recovery can take weeks or even months, depending on the circumstances. Your immediate goal is to stop additional fraud, protect your information and create a record of what happened. What to do in the first 24 hours after identity theft The following checklist breaks the process into manageable steps. The time frames are guidelines, so prioritize active fraud and compromised accounts rather than waiting for a particular hour. Hour 1: Stop the immediate damage Start with the accounts most likely to expose your money or personal information. Important: If money has been stolen, report it to your financial institution immediately. Federal protections and reporting deadlines vary by account and transaction type. Hours 2 to 4: Protect your credit Next, make it harder for criminals to open additional accounts using your personal information. You can freeze your credit even if you expect to apply for a loan or credit card soon. Simply lift the freeze temporarily when necessary. Hours 4 to 8: Report the identity theft Creating an official record can help you dispute fraudulent accounts and recover your identity. An FTC identity theft report can help you exercise certain rights under federal law, including requesting that credit bureaus block fraudulent information. However, you generally do not need to file an FTC report before notifying a bank about unauthorized transactions. A SCAMMER HAS YOUR NAME, PHONE NUMBER AND ADDRESS. WHAT CAN THEY ACTUALLY DO? Hours 8 to 16: Secure your other accounts Identity thieves sometimes try to use stolen information across multiple services. Hours 16 to 24: Document everything Once you've addressed the most urgent threats, organize your recovery efforts. Common identity theft recovery mistakes to avoid Even when you're moving quickly, certain mistakes can create additional problems. 9 WARNING SIGNS OF IDENTITY THEFT YOU SHOULD NEVER IGNORE What can wait beyond the first day Some recovery tasks will continue beyond the first day, including disputing fraudulent accounts, correcting credit reports and following up with creditors. However, report unauthorized financial transactions immediately. Federal protections and reporting deadlines vary depending on the type of account and transaction. Your initial priority is to stop additional fraud and secure your information. How identity theft protection can add another layer of security Recovering from identity theft often involves contacting multiple financial institutions, disputing fraudulent charges and keeping track of important paperwork. If you're helping someone else through this Many people go through this first-24-hours checklist not for themselves, but for an aging parent, a spouse or another family member. If you're the one helping, the same steps apply. Start by securing compromised accounts, freezing credit, reporting fraud and documenting what happened. Keep in mind that you may need permission or legal authorization to speak with financial institutions on someone else's behalf. Patience is important, too. Identity theft can be frightening, especially for someone who isn't comfortable managing financial accounts online. Helping them make phone calls, organize paperwork and track important deadlines can make the recovery process easier. In the days that follow Once the first 24 hours are behind you, continue working through your checklist. Dispute fraudulent charges and accounts, follow up on your identity theft report and request that fraudulent information be removed from your credit reports. Keep monitoring your financial accounts for suspicious activity, since criminals may attempt additional fraud using stolen information. Recovery timelines vary depending on the type and extent of the theft. Some problems can be resolved quickly, while more complicated cases may take months. Consider asking a trusted family member or close friend to help you stay organized. Having someone review documents, take notes or track deadlines can help prevent important details from slipping through the cracks. The most important thing is to stay focused on what you can control. Secure your accounts, report suspicious activity promptly and follow through on unresolved disputes. You may not fix everything in the first 24 hours, but taking these steps can help limit further damage and put you on the path to recovery. I've seen how quickly one compromised account can lead to bigger problems, especially when criminals get access to email or other personal information. My advice is to focus on what you can control right away. Contact your bank, secure your most important accounts and freeze your credit with all three bureaus. Then report the theft and keep a record of every conversation. You don't need to pay a company to take these initial steps. I also recommend keeping an eye on your accounts long after the first day. articles.title: How much of your earnings are subject to Social Security tax in 2027?
articles.summary: The amount of your pay subject to Social Security tax has increased for 2027.
articles.body:
With Social Security announcing its annual cost-of-living adjustment for 2027 this week, the program also released new income thresholds subject to payroll taxes next year.

Social Security benefits are funded through payroll taxes, which are then invested in trust funds and paid out in monthly checks to millions of retirees and Americans with disabilities.

The tax only applies to earnings up to a yearly cap. Next year, the maximum amount of earnings subject to the Social Security tax in 2027 will jump to $192,300, up from $184,500 this year.

Here's how the math breaks down: Workers and their employers each pay 6.2% on wages up to that amount. If you're self-employed, you pay the entire amount — 12.4%.

That means the maximum Social Security withholding for a worker next year will be $23,842, or 12.4% of $192,300. Any income above that amount is not subject to the Social Security tax.

The backdrop: Social Security's reserves could run out at the end of 2032. At that point, if no adjustments are made, the entitlement program's Old-Age and Survivors Insurance (OASI) Trust Fund will be able to pay out only about 80% of benefits to seniors, according to the 2026 Social Security and Medicare Trustees' annual report.

Raising that earnings tax cap, or eliminating it, has been a contentious debate in Washington in the quest to address the future of Social Security.

Lawmakers have floated a range of fixes, from raising payroll taxes to increasing the retirement age for younger workers to lifting the cap on earnings subject to Social Security taxes.

"Congress has only two options to address the projected shortfall," Nancy Altman, president of Social Security Works, a nonprofit advocacy organization, told Yahoo Finance. "Bring more money into Social Security, or cut benefits."

One proposal that has attracted some bipartisan attention: Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio have introduced legislation to eliminate the income cap on contributions to Social Security.

As they wrote in their New York Times op-ed in July: "This is a no-brainer: The wealthiest Americans, who have benefited the most from America's opportunities, should contribute the same percentage of their income as a factory worker in Chillicothe, Ohio, or a teacher in Worcester, Mass."

articles.title: Trump posts AI-edited photo to brag about White House restoration work
articles.summary: President Donald Trump appears to have posted an AI-edited photo that shows a “renovated” White House column.
articles.body: President Donald Trump posted a series of photos on Truth Social showing off renovations to the White House — but one of them appears to be modified with AI. The picture, which compares an old White House column to a “restored” one, has several discrepancies and was flagged by Google’s AI detector as “made or edited with OpenAI.” As pointed out by users on Reddit, the picture of the “restored” column has an uneven number of steps on both sides of the structure. The number of steps also doesn’t match up with the ones in the “before” photo. Additionally, the before and after photos appear nearly identical in angle and detail; the reflection in the windows is nearly the same, and the protective cardboard at the bottom of the column seems to be in the same spot as well. Not to mention that the “newly-painted” one looks unnaturally smooth. [Image: Google’s SynthID detector flagged it as made or edited with OpenAI’s tools. The Verge can confirm that the photo posted to Truth Social is flagged as AI-generated when uploaded to Google’s SynthID Detector, which scans images, videos, and audio for an invisible watermark that indicates it was “created or edited” with AI. Real pictures show people painting the front of the White House in June, so it’s possible the column actually did get a fresh coat of paint — the White House didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. The SynthID watermark wasn’t detected on other pictures Trump posted, which show the White House facade and heliport. Trump is no stranger to AI tools, though, as he often posts AI-generated caricatures of himself, while the White House has been known to post racist AI memes and at least one photo deceptively edited to make a protester appear distraught.

articles.title: Questions flare over US role in Ukraine’s Starlink shut-off: What to know
articles.summary: On Wednesday, Elon Musk’s Starlink was pulled into the center of a controversy after Ukraine’s military faced restricted access to Starshield, the military version of the satellite-based system. Starlink services were cut off for objects that traveled more than 100 mph, impacting the capabilities of Ukraine’s drones, airplanes and helicopters, a source familiar with the…
articles.body:
On Wednesday, Elon Musk’s Starlink was pulled into the center of a controversy after Ukraine’s military faced restricted access to Starshield, the military version of the satellite-based system.

Starlink services were cut off for objects that traveled more than 100 mph, impacting the capabilities of Ukraine’s drones, airplanes and helicopters, a source familiar with the matter told The Hill .

In an interview Wednesday with Piers Morgan, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the loss of access a “big mistake.”

“People will die, of course, if attacks will continue and if Starlink will not work … it’s not helpful,” he said.

Senators demand answers and accountability

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) publicly called on Musk to explain the loss of fast data speeds that Ukraine needs for its military operations.

In a social media post Wednesday, the North Carolina senator asked Musk for assurances on whether the disruptions to Starlink were unintended and that SpaceX is trying to fix the glitch.

Tillis further warned “intentionally degrading Ukraine’s ability to defend itself might be construed as aiding and abetting a mass murderer,” referring to Russian President Vladimir Putin.

In another post late Wednesday , Tillis said he will be asking the Pentagon’s inspector general to start an investigation and report back to Congress.

“The latest reporting suggests this strategic snafu may have occurred more locally within DOD Starshield systems, not with Starlink or SpaceX,” he wrote in his post, referring to the Department of Defense.

“At best, this was an unacceptable error or lapse, and at worst a conscience decision to clear the field for a Russian attack,” he added.

Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), who played a major part in passing a tough new Russia sanctions bill , took to social platform X on Wednesday to demand accountability.

“Reports of Starlink failing in Ukraine are deeply alarming— potentially crippling air defense against Russia’s murderous missiles & drones. Trump & Musk must be held accountable,” he wrote.

Musk says the decision is up to the president

As confusion erupted, the SpaceX CEO said Wednesday that the decisions to restrict the speed or usage of Starlink’s Starshield are made by the U.S. military and, ultimately, the president.

“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk wrote in a comment on X.

“Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company,” he added.

Mykhailo Fedorov, Ukraine’s former minister of defense, said Wednesday afternoon that the country’s connectivity with Starlink was being restored at speeds of up to 160 km per hour. He thanked Musk for the returned speed and wrote, “We hope for your continued support.”

Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.), an Air Force veteran, said the recent moves, including reports that the U.S. has stopped sharing intelligence with Kyiv, are helping an invader, referring to Putin.

“The Administration’s decision to reduce intel sharing to Ukraine & access to Starlink equates to aiding the invader & the war criminal who bombs cities,” Bacon wrote in a post on X.

“Does the Administration think it will get ANY support for the remainder of the 119th Congress? Their agenda is dead unless they change paths,” he added.

articles.title: A ciência pode nos fazer viver mais? Entenda os limites da busca pela longevidade  | G1
articles.standfirst: Em laboratórios espalhados pelo mundo, cientistas investigam desde terapias genéticas capazes de corrigir falhas no DNA até tratamentos voltados para eliminar células associadas ao envelhecimento.
articles.summary: Em laboratórios espalhados pelo mundo, cientistas investigam desde terapias genéticas capazes de corrigir falhas no DNA até tratamentos voltados para eliminar células associadas ao envelhecimento.
articles.body:
Viver mais e com mais saúde é um dos maiores objetivos da medicina moderna. Em laboratórios espalhados pelo mundo, cientistas investigam desde terapias genéticas capazes de corrigir falhas no DNA até tratamentos voltados para eliminar células associadas ao envelhecimento. Mas, apesar dos avanços, especialistas alertam que existe uma diferença importante entre aumentar a qualidade de vida e prometer uma espécie de juventude eterna.

O debate ganhou força nos últimos anos com o surgimento de empresários e investidores dispostos a gastar milhões de dólares em pesquisas sobre longevidade. Um dos casos mais conhecidos é o do empresário americano Brian Johnson, que mantém uma rotina intensa de dietas, suplementos e exames com o objetivo de reduzir sua idade biológica e retardar os efeitos do envelhecimento.

Para muitos cientistas, porém, a ideia de interromper completamente o envelhecimento ainda está longe da realidade. Segundo especialistas ouvidos pela série Código da Vida, há um limite biológico para a vida humana, e promessas de fazer pessoas viverem até 140 anos ou mais encontram pouco respaldo nas evidências científicas atuais.

As principais pesquisas sobre longevidade hoje se concentram em entender os mecanismos que levam ao envelhecimento das células.

Uma das linhas de investigação busca corrigir problemas nas mitocôndrias, estruturas responsáveis pela produção de energia celular. Outra estuda maneiras de identificar e eliminar as chamadas células senescentes, que deixam de funcionar corretamente e se acumulam no organismo com o passar do tempo. Essas células são frequentemente descritas como "células zumbis" porque permanecem no corpo mesmo após perderem sua função original.

Há também uma forte aposta nas terapias genéticas. Pesquisadores trabalham em técnicas de edição do DNA capazes de corrigir mutações responsáveis por doenças hereditárias. Em alguns casos, o objetivo é alterar apenas uma única "letra" do código genético para restaurar a função normal das células.

Pesquisadores afirmam que a correção de erros genéticos já vem produzindo resultados animadores em doenças raras. Nos Estados Unidos, equipes trabalham em tratamentos para doenças hereditárias da visão utilizando técnicas de edição genética aplicadas diretamente nos olhos.

Outra área de destaque é a biologia sintética. Cientistas desenvolvem moléculas chamadas XNAs, capazes de desempenhar funções semelhantes às do DNA, mas com estrutura química diferente. A expectativa é que elas possam ser utilizadas no desenvolvimento de novos medicamentos e terapias avançadas.

Pesquisas em xenobiologia também tentam criar proteínas artificiais produzidas com aminoácidos de laboratório. Segundo os pesquisadores, essas moléculas poderão futuramente ser utilizadas no tratamento de doenças degenerativas, na produção de novos antibióticos e até em aplicações relacionadas ao envelhecimento celular.

Por que a imortalidade ainda está distante

Apesar do entusiasmo, especialistas lembram que a maioria dessas tecnologias ainda está em fase experimental. Um dos maiores desafios é garantir que os tratamentos sejam eficazes e seguros.

Casos recentes envolvendo terapias genéticas experimentais na China mostraram os riscos dessa corrida. Em dois estudos que utilizavam variantes da técnica de edição genética CRISPR, pacientes morreram poucos dias após o tratamento. Segundo pesquisadores, o problema esteve relacionado ao uso de vírus modificados para transportar as moléculas terapêuticas até as células do organismo.

Os episódios reforçaram a avaliação de que, embora os avanços sejam promissores, ainda será necessário superar importantes obstáculos científicos antes que essas tecnologias possam ser oferecidas em larga escala.

Para os pesquisadores, o objetivo mais realista não é tornar os seres humanos imortais, mas prolongar o período de vida com saúde. A expectativa é que, nas próximas décadas, tratamentos genéticos ajudem a prevenir doenças, corrigir mutações e substituir medicamentos de uso contínuo por intervenções mais precisas e duradouras.

A busca pela longevidade continua avançando, mas o consenso entre os cientistas é que viver mais dependerá menos de soluções milagrosas e mais da combinação entre pesquisa de longo prazo, avanços médicos e um entendimento cada vez maior sobre o funcionamento do próprio corpo humano.

articles.title: Warsh Boosts Market Expectations of Fed Hold in October
articles.summary: Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh did nothing to dispel market expectations that the US central bank will hold interest rates steady when it meets at the...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh did nothing to dispel market expectations that the US central bank will hold interest rates steady when it meets at the end of the month.

In a moderated discussion Friday morning in Bangkok at the International Monetary Fund's annual meetings, Warsh made no remarks on monetary policy or his outlook for the US economy, save for reiterating that the Fed will deliver price stability.

"We made very clear that we would deliver price stability, and we removed a dose of accommodation about a month ago," Warsh said. "I don't prejudge meetings. I don't believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year."

Investors pared their bets for a rate hike at the central bank's Oct. 27-28 policy gathering. The odds, which were hovering around 27% before Warsh spoke, dropped below 15% following his remarks.

"It was clear that he wasn't going to deliver anything that the market could latch on to as hawkish," Derek Tang, an economist at Monetary Policy Analytics, wrote in a note to clients.

The Fed raised interest rates by a quarter percentage point in September, the first hike since 2023. It was backed by all 19 policymakers, and a majority also saw another increase as likely this year.

A few key officials in recent weeks reiterated that additional rate hikes may be needed, but emphasized they have time to gather economic data before acting again.

Warsh repeated his bullish views on artificial intelligence, calling it the most important innovation in the global economy during his lifetime. But he also warned that it may be driving demand in the near term.

The Fed chief said that as a central banker, he's taking the new technology seriously but also "soberly, responsibly."

"It's obviously hitting the demand side of the economy before it's going to hit the supply side of the economy," Warsh said. "If you're a central banker, you're in the business of trying to ensure stable prices and full employment, you've got to recognize this as a shock."

While it's a positive supply shock in the medium term, Warsh argued, it's driving increases in aggregate demand now.

Some of Warsh's colleagues have expressed similar concerns, even questioning whether the surge in investment that's buoying the AI build-out could lead to an overheating of the economy.

articles.title: Hegseth ramps up US troops in Panama as Pentagon expands war on drug cartels
articles.summary: The Pentagon is sending more U.S. troops to Panama to participate in jungle warfare training as Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth expands the U.S. military’s war against drug cartels in Latin America. Nearly 200 Army soldiers from Fort Drum, a U.S. Army military reservation in northern New York state, are being sent to a jungle training…
articles.body:
The Pentagon is sending more U.S. troops to Panama to participate in jungle warfare training as Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth expands the U.S. military’s war against drug cartels in Latin America.

Nearly 200 Army soldiers from Fort Drum, a U.S. Army military reservation in northern New York state, are being sent to a jungle training facility in the Central American nation to prepare in survival and combat tactics.

They will not be conducting counter-narcotics training, according to one U.S. official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal military deliberations.

Upon completing the multiweek training course, the troops will return to the U.S., the official told The Hill on Thursday. The official said the troops may partake in additional training with Honduran, Colombian and Guatemalan forces.

The U.S. Southern Command (Southcom), which oversees U.S. military operations in Central and South America, declined to comment.

When The Hill reached out to Hegseth’s office for comment, a Pentagon official said the Bilateral Jungle Operations Training, a program where U.S. and Panamanian forces train together in jungle terrain, reflects the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition (A3C) “collaboration, complementary capabilities and persistent engagement with allies and partners.”

“This sharpens the capabilities of U.S. and partner nation troops in harsh jungle environments like the remote areas in which cartels hide,” the Pentagon official said. “These activities reflect the ongoing A3C approach of working with capable allies and partners to deepen collaboration and maintain persistent pressure against hemispheric threat networks.”

“For operational security reasons, we do not discuss specific force posture, movement timelines, unit disposition, or mission details,” the official said.

The U.S. military revived jungle warfare training alongside Panamanian security forces last fall for the first time in more than 20 years. In the training, service members perform weapons drills and learn survival techniques, including how to purify water, navigate the thick vegetation and build shelters, The Hill reported last year.

The training — which has been done by members of the Army, Marine Corps, Air Force and Space Force — has been at Base Aeronaval Cristóbal Colón, a naval base formerly known as Fort Sherman.

“We’re really looking at this as that interoperability training, where both of us are growing in our knowledge down here,” Army Maj. Cody McBroom said in an interview at the time. “So as we ramp this up, and obviously it’s what we can support, what they can support to make sure it’s mutually benefiting for both of us.”

Lee Schlenker, a research associate with the Global South program at the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, said the administration is right to focus on Latin America, and to provide aid to governments on security issues.

But he questioned whether the deployment could lead to unintended consequences.

“While the administration is right to focus on its near abroad and provide regional governments with support to tackle pressing security challenges, surging troop deployments without proper Congressional authorization or a clearly stated legal rationale risks leading us into an interminable war against a shifting set of targets with no clear entry or exit strategy,” he said.

He also said the efforts could do “remarkably little to address the drivers of the drug trade.”

He described the drivers as “surging demand, public corruption, lack of formal employment and deficient judicial and law enforcement institutions.”

The New York Times first reported on the deployment , but the U.S. embassy in Panama pushed back, calling the deployment of 600 U.S. troops “ categorically false .”

The embassy said 120 service members from the 10th Mountain Division, based at Fort Drum, are participating in a two-week jungle warfare training course in Panama. Upon completing the training on Oct. 25, they will head back to home base at Fort Drum.

Other service members will partake in regional exercises, including Southern Vanguard, an annual bilateral and multilateral military exercise sponsored by Southcom in Peru, the embassy said in a statement.

Last month, U.S. soldiers trained alongside Peruvian and Chilean forces during Southern Vanguard.

The deployment of troops for training in Panama comes as the Pentagon continues to ramp up its multifront war against drug cartels in South America and as the Trump administration is pushing Latin American nations to team up with U.S. forces in joint operations against alleged drug traffickers.

The U.S. military has been blowing up alleged drug boats in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific, strikes that have come under scrutiny by Democratic lawmakers and have been panned as summary executions by some law of war experts.

The U.S. military has also started interdicting larger refueling vessels off the coast of Ecuador before destroying them. U.S. forces recently have also begun embedding on the ground with Ecuadorian authorities in raids against alleged drug traffickers, a new dimension in Southcom’s campaign against criminal groups designated as foreign terrorist organizations.

“Based on our assessment of what needs to be done, this plan focuses on five core lines of effort: dismantling illicit networks, attacking network logistics, preventing adversary regeneration, bolstering partner sovereignty and security, and building a strong coalition,” Southcom Commander Gen. Francis L. Donovan said in a recent interview with The Hill when talking about Southcom’s “Offensive Campaign Plan.”

To help execute the plan, the U.S. has formed a coalition of 19 nations in Central and South America with the goal of wiping out drug cartels, and the Pentagon sent MQ-9 Reaper drones — armed with precision weapons, wide-range sensors and multimode communications suite — to the Southcom theater.

The U.S. military conducted land strikes in South America earlier this year. Those strikes and on-the-ground raids will ramp up as the capabilities of those nations rise, a senior Pentagon official recently told The Hill. Honduras and Guatemala have sent letters asking for joint operations with U.S. forces.

Donovan completed a 3-day visit to Peru on Thursday, alongside U.S. Ambassador to Peru Bernie Navarro, where they met with Peruvian Defense Minister Rafael Belaúnde Llosa and Gen. César Augusto Briceño Valdivia, the Chief of the Joint Command of the Armed Forces

The meetings focused on “joint efforts to combat narco-terrorists” and hemispheric threat networks. The leaders on both sides laid the groundwork for “greater cooperation” to combat these criminal groups in the Valle de los Ríos Apurímac, Southcom said .

Earlier this month, Hegseth indicated that some U.S. troops could be redeployed from Europe to the Western Hemisphere, emphasizing the U.S. military is at “war” with drug cartels.

There are efforts to send more personnel, assets and other financial resources to the Western Hemisphere, and there have been discussions inside the Pentagon about deploying more U.S. service members to Southcom, the senior Pentagon official previously said.
