articles.title: Staying connected under fire: How GSAT-7C will boost IAF's fighting edge
articles.summary: The Indian Air Force will receive a dedicated communications satellite to strengthen its network-centric warfare capabilities under a Rs 2,563 crore deal
articles.body: The Indian Air Force will receive a dedicated communications satellite to strengthen its network-centric warfare capabilities under a Rs 2,563 crore deal signed with NewSpace India Limited.The indigenously designed, developed and manufactured GSAT-7C is intended to provide more secure and resilient communications for the service. Its significance lies not merely in adding another satellite to orbit, but in strengthening the communications network that allows aircraft, radars and command centres to share information and coordinate operations in real time.Network-centric warfare connects sensors, command centres, communications systems and weapon platforms, enabling information to be shared and acted upon simultaneously. A fighter jet may detect a target, a ground-based radar may track an approaching aircraft, and a command centre may coordinate the response. If these elements cannot exchange information reliably, commanders are left with an incomplete picture of the battlefield, while forces struggle to coordinate their actions.Satellite communications can help bridge these gaps, particularly when operations extend beyond the reach of direct radio links or when terrestrial networks are unavailable or inadequate because of distance, terrain or other limitations.GSAT-7C is intended to support this capability through software-defined radios. The Defence Acquisition Council cleared the project on November 23, 2021, at an initial cost of Rs 2,236 crore for the satellite and associated ground hubs. The stated objective was to enable real-time connectivity for software-defined radios and secure beyond-line-of-sight communications for the armed forces.Unlike conventional radios, which rely heavily on dedicated hardware for specific functions, software-defined radios use software to perform many of these tasks. This allows their operating modes and waveforms to be modified or updated without requiring a separate radio for every communication requirement. When integrated with satellite links, compatible radios can exchange information over long distances, extending communications beyond the range of conventional radio networks.For the IAF, this capability could improve coordination across a widely dispersed network of aircraft, radar installations and airborne early warning platforms. A fighter operating far from its base, for instance, may need to exchange information with other aircraft or command centres beyond direct radio range. An additional space-based communications link could help maintain these connections, supporting the faster flow of information between operational units and decision-makers.The IAF already has a dedicated communications satellite, GSAT-7A, launched by the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) on December 19, 2018. Operating in the Ku band, it provides communications coverage over the Indian region and has been described in defence reporting as linking aircraft, radar stations, airbases and airborne early warning platforms.GSAT-7C will add to this space-based communications capability, although its precise relationship with GSAT-7A remains unclear.The government has not publicly disclosed whether the new satellite will use the same frequency bands, coverage configuration or payload architecture. GSAT-7A was designed for an eight-year mission life, placing it around the end of that period in December 2026. However, reaching the end of a satellite's designed mission life does not necessarily mean it must immediately cease operating.Greater connectivity, however, also creates vulnerabilities. As armed forces become increasingly dependent on connected sensors, aircraft and command systems, their communications links become potential targets for jamming, interference and cyberattacks. Satellite services and ground infrastructure can also be targeted in attempts to disrupt the flow of information on which military operations depend.The stated emphasis on secure and resilient communications is therefore central to GSAT-7C's intended role. The satellite's actual resilience will depend on the security and design of the wider communications system, including encryption, anti-jamming capabilities, redundancy, protected ground infrastructure and alternative communication routes. The objective is not simply to connect more platforms, but to ensure that the network remains usable even when an adversary attempts to disrupt it.The Ministry of Defence's announcement does not specify a launch date, payload details, frequency bands or coverage area. It also does not explain the increase in the contract value to Rs 2,563 crore from the initial approval of Rs 2,236 crore in 2021.

articles.title: The first vibe-coded gun is here
articles.summary: The creator of the first functional 3D-printed gun Cody Wilson says he’s made an AI model that generates ‘unique’ gun designs. Gun control experts are concerned.
articles.body: Since gun-rights activist and alt-right-friendly agitator Cody Wilson made the first 3D-printed firearm 13 years ago, he’s helped usher in a chaotic era of untraceable ghost guns. Now he’s claiming another first: “the first AI-made gun.” It’s called the WASP. I stood about 20 feet away as Wilson and his sidekick clamped the WASP to a DIY test mount outside Defense Distributed headquarters in Austin, Texas. The 3D-printed .22 caliber handgun is, in reality, little more than a pistol barrel attached to a spring-loaded plastic box. Its rudimentary design bears a resemblance to Wilson’s single-shot 3D-printed “Liberator,” albeit with some quintessentially AI-generated oddities, like a wacky, bubbly grip that doesn’t quite fit a human hand. It was aimed toward a shallow green slope in the backyard of a semi-residential neighborhood. A long black string ran from its trigger to Wilson, who sat crouched about 10 feet back behind a police riot shield. “Three. Two. One.” I braced for a thunderous crack, but instead heard only a loud click. The world’s first AI-generated gun had misfired. “This didn’t happen last time,” Wilson, annoyed, reassured me as he carried out some quick troubleshooting. The gun’s striker had hit the cartridge, he said, but failed to set off the primer. I quietly took another step back. After some more fiddling, Wilson declared the WASP ready for a second chance. This time, pulling the string produced a sharp bang, about as loud as a firecracker. Downrange, a cardboard target had a hole ripped through its top left corner. His colleague had suggested using a life-size cutout of Joe Biden, but Wilson shot that down as “too on the nose.” The safety test completed, Wilson then unclamped the WASP, slipped on a protective glove, took aim at the cardboard target, and squeezed the trigger himself. Another bang. This time, a miss, slightly high. The AI gun, today at least, was two for three in terms of shots successfully fired. [Image: A hand-drawn target in the backyard of the Defense Distributed headquarters in Austin, Texas. With the smell of gunpowder still lingering, I asked Wilson the obvious question: Why make this functionally suspect firearm in the first place? We’re in Texas, where buying a conventional gun is often easier than getting a driver’s license. He paused, taking issue with the premise. “I would argue that what we’ve made is not an AI-generated gun, but an AI that can generate guns.” His supposed AI gunsmith is a custom model he calls GatGPT. But instead of generating pasta recipes or travel plans, this unfiltered model answers questions about firearms. It’s trained on DEFCAD’s expansive library of gun files and can help enthusiasts pick out the exact parts they need for a build. Launched in 2012, DEFCAD (another Wilson-led project) is the world’s largest online repository of digital gun and component files. Gun safety advocates and lawmakers have argued sites like DEFCAD aid the proliferation of “ghost guns,” firearms made partly or entirely of components without a serial number. Wilson, meanwhile, has called access to firearms “a fundamental human right.” Under US federal law, licensed gun makers are required to include serial numbers on the frames or receivers of guns they sell. Wilson and others in what’s referred to as the 3D2A movement say gun files aren’t actually guns, they are computer code, a form of protected speech. That core argument, whether or not gun codes are protected speech, has been argued in court cases for over a decade, with many often citing or involving Wilson. It’s possible the issue will wind up before the Supreme Court. Now, Wilson claims, AI can also come up with its own unique designs. The results have a bizarre, surrealist quality emblematic of early generative art to the tune of Will Smith slurping spaghetti. The WASP’s entire development, Wilson claims, from its name to safety tweaks (an early grip design could have cost someone a finger), resulted from a natural-language dialogue between the model and its human user. In other words, it’s essentially a vibe-coded gun. Though mostly a proof of concept, the WASP nonetheless fires real, lethal rounds and doesn’t have a serial number. Wilson believes AI-generated guns like this will only improve as GatGPT ingests more data, and as users engage with it. But the WASP also poses another pressing public safety issue. Producing 3D-printed guns has gotten easier over the years, but it still fundamentally requires some technical know-how. Now, however, a novice armed with GatGPT could plausibly make a gun with only a handful of prompts. That’s exactly the kind of barrier-lowering that critics of 3D-printed guns, like Everytown, have spent years warning about. “[Wilson] admits the goal here,” Everytown senior vice president for law and policy Justin Wagner told The Verge. “He wants to lower the barrier to entry so anyone, regardless of their background check status or legal eligibility [can] own a gun. He wants anyone to be able to design and manufacture weapons, and that’s dangerous.” Everytown has played a prominent role in advocating for a pair of recently passed laws in New York and California that will require 3D printer manufacturers to install firearm-blocking software that can detect guns or gun parts and stop them before they are ever printed. (Experts have questioned how and if these methods would actually work.) Wilson didn’t specifically cite evading detection as a reason for building an AI gun maker, but the development comes on the heels of his recent efforts to complicate firearm-blocking technology that New York and California will require in future 3D printers. In August, Wilson began rolling out a tool called Hochulization (a jab at New York Gov. Kathy Hochul) that he says subtly alters a file’s underlying hash, which functions as a kind of digital fingerprint. By late September, Wilson claimed to The Verge that users had already “Hochulized” files more than 26,000 times, with some users applying the treatment more than once. It’s one of the many ways Wilson has planted a flag in the evolving battle over how to regulate 3D-printed guns. The core idea behind that “self-defense measure,” as Wilson calls it, is to stymie a purely hash-based gun detection system by rendering it unable to keep up with constantly changing hashes. A new AI-generated gun design also wouldn’t immediately be recognized in a gun detection database, since it didn’t exist yet. More sophisticated gun detection software goes beyond simple hashes and uses AI to try to predict whether a file is likely a gun or gun component before it prints. It’s unclear whether this type of software, which is still being developed, would reliably detect a sufficiently strange-looking AI-generated gun design. “Individuals who intentionally aim to thwart safety regulations put themselves and New York communities at risk, which is why Gov. Hochul remains committed to combating emerging threats and the production of ghost guns and illegally manufactured guns, and strengthening regulations that keep New Yorkers safe,” Hochul spokesperson Jess D’Amelia told The Verge. Defense Distributed’s AI didn’t just log on one day and suddenly decide to build a gun. It started with a specific request from a human to riff off an existing design. An employee asked the model to build a new gun based on a design called “Ergo Harlot,” itself a variation of the more popular “Harlot” model. Like the WASP, the Harlot is a compact single-shot handgun that fires a .22 caliber round. The AI prompter, according to chat logs viewed by The Verge, framed the assignment as a “challenge” and told the AI model its entry “must be completely and fully functional and have a unique design.” Chat logs show the AI model responding with a plan for a new design called the WASP and submitting it for approval. The AI didn’t explain its name choice, though Wilson suggested it bears some physical resemblance to the insect. When I asked whether it’s possibly an abbreviation for “white Anglo-Saxon protestant,” he said it isn’t. The AI model listed six key changes it made to the inspiration design, including a slightly longer barrel than the Harlot’s and a grip made of three grooved, circular lobes. Once a Defense Distributed employee approved the model’s plan, the logs show it checking and testing each component, much like how an AI coding agent such as Anthropic’s Claude Code works through a checklist when vibe-coding an app. The team then printed the WASP in its office on a Bambu Lab printer using standard plastic filaments, along with a handful of common metal parts for the firing pin and barrel. Wilson said the print took about six hours. So is the WASP actually a good gun? Ashley Hlebinsky, a firearms historian and founder of consulting firm The Gun Code, told The Verge that it’s hard to judge without handling it, but several design choices stand out as odd. Most notably, the AI appears to have started making a trigger guard (the loop that normally protects a shooter’s finger) but doesn’t finish it, leaving the trigger exposed, for no apparent reason. The gun also seems to borrow from what are called modern “beavertail” grip designs. But bizarrely, the AI appears to have inverted its grip. “It reminds me of times when I’ve prompted AI to draw a picture of a gun and it gets most of the way there but then has some weird parts missing,” Hlebinsky said. “It has an obvious futuristic, sci-fi appearance that reminds me of Marvin the Martian’s ray gun.” Jonathan Ferguson, keeper of firearms and artillery at the Royal Armories Museum in Leeds, England, was more critical when asked if the WASP seemed functional. “Functional? From a legal perspective, if it successfully fires a shot without a breech explosion, it’s a viable firearm, but so are two lengths of steel pipe with a firing pin and cap attached to the rear of one,” Ferguson told The Verge. “From a technical perspective, I would not call this a ‘sound’ or ‘good’ firearm. It does not appear to be comfortable to hold or easy to aim and, based on the test firing, seems to be only marginally functional.” If anything, Ferguson noted, he expected generative AI in 2026 to do a better job at designing a reliable firearm. “There are vestigial sights that can’t work, an open trigger guard, [and a] weirdly shaped grip.” “This certainly is a development, [but] I don’t think it’s necessarily that novel. It’s another way to 3D print a gun,” Wagner said. “A victim of a mass shooting who was shot by a ghost gun told me when you get shot, it doesn’t matter if it’s a ghost gun, a 3D-printed gun, or a gun that got bought over the counter. They’re all just as lethal,” he added. Wilson is confident his AI’s design will improve, both in terms of functionality and aesthetic uniqueness, as the DEFCAD database grows. More gun files will help, but he expects the biggest gains will come from users chatting with the model and pushing it to refine its choices. (GatGPT is currently in limited early access.) Eventually, he predicts, constant back-and-forth between users and AI could dramatically speed up the pace at which new 3D-printed gun designs appear. “This is all just spontaneous parallel thinking,” Wilson said. “I think you’ll see those cycles faster now because of AI.” “It’s like you’re speedrunning the available possibilities, the materials, the platforms, the concepts,” he added. A skeptic would say the WASP’s origins as essentially a remix of a previous designs makes its claims to true originality shaky. Like many half-baked AI movie scripts or janky generative art, the WASP conjures up the familiar feeling of AI slop, made manifest in the real world. Even Wilson admits it looks a bit like a “Fortnite gun.” Still, Wilson maintains the WASP is fundamentally an AI creation and one that he’s ultimately not responsible for, even though his team’s prompts led to its creation. That position aligns with a broader argument Wilson’s made for the better part of a decade in legal skirmishes with the State Department and local lawmakers: that gun files are protected speech. In fact, Wilson said he doesn’t necessarily consider the WASP a gun at all until it’s printed and fired. “This thing lives first as a digital organism,” he said.

articles.title: Meta’s new terms may allow it to train AI on news sites for free
articles.summary: Meta’s new terms for business accounts appear to give it permission to scrape online publications for free, as reported by Nieman Lab.
articles.body: Meta’s new terms appear to give it permission to crawl and scrape websites “associated” with the businesses that use its platforms — including online publishers, according to a report from Nieman Lab. The new terms, which go into effect on October 30th, say Meta can use this outside content to “develop, improve, research,” and “train” its AI products. While Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts says that the company is just “consolidating” its commercial and self-serve ad terms, legal experts tell Nieman Lab that this could allow Meta “to argue its commercial terms supersede other blocking instructions,” like a site’s robots.txt file. That could potentially allow Meta to bypass a licensing agreement and freely train its AI models on content posted by online publishers. The new policy applies to business accounts that promote their content across Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Messenger: > You authorize us (or any entity acting on our behalf) to use automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents) and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs (and any content available through them) that are associated with your products or services, or that are made available through your or users’ use of Meta Company Products and services, and to periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages, or URLs. Meta may use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services, and features provided under these Commercial Terms and any other applicable supplemental terms. Roberts pushes back on Nieman Lab’s reporting, saying “There is no change to how Meta uses web crawlers; any suggestion to the contrary is false… Content owners can still use robots.txt flags to indicate their preferences, as we clearly explain in our developer documentation.” Meta has followed OpenAI in striking AI licensing deals with CNN, Fox News, USA Today, and People Inc., but these terms could give the company access to a much broader swath of content. “For news publishers, this clearly represents permission to Meta to train AI on any content from their sites and possibly to deploy some of that content, even in competition with the publishers themselves,” James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell, tells Nieman Lab. Andy Stone, Meta’s vice president of communications, writes in a post on X that this change isn’t meant to target news sites. “This update is designed to make sure we’re able to pull accurate information about products for sale on third-party websites when making on-platform ad and content recommendations, not about scraping news sites.” Businesses that don’t agree to Meta’s new policies “may stop all access or use of our Products for business or commercial purposes,” the terms say. Last month, Meta launched a new Meta One subscription that requires businesses and creators to pay to include links in posts and reels. “Put another way, Meta has begun charging users to post links to the same content that it will be permitted to crawl for free,” Nieman Lab says. Update, October 16th: Added a statement from Meta and legal commentary.

articles.title: Amazon About You may know you a little too well
articles.summary: Amazon's About You feature includes personality details from your shopping history, and some shoppers are finding hilariously awkward results.
articles.body: Amazon knows what you buy, what you search for and even what you tell its shopping assistant. Now, the company is giving you a look at the personality profile it has built from all that information. When I checked my own Amazon About You profile, I found 81 results, including a reference to my mother that caught me off guard. The feature brings together details about your shopping habits and preferences. Some are helpful. Others might make you wonder how Amazon reached those conclusions in the first place. Shoppers are now sharing screenshots of descriptions that range from funny to completely inaccurate. Amazon says the feature helps improve shopping recommendations. However, it also raises an interesting privacy question. How much should a retailer know about you, and how much control do you really have over that information? Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Join us Saturday, October 31, at 11 AM ET / 8 AM PT. Register free now at CyberGuyLive.com. WHAT YOUR INTERNET PROVIDER, WEBSITES AND ADVERTISERS SEE What is Amazon About You? Amazon introduced About You in May 2026, although the feature has recently attracted widespread attention as shoppers share their profiles on social media. Amazon has personalized shopping recommendations for years. If you bought a coffee maker, you probably noticed suggestions for filters or other accessories soon afterward. That kind of recommendation has become familiar to anyone who shops online. Now, Amazon is taking personalization further with About You, a section that shows shoppers what the company believes about their interests and preferences. According to Amazon's announcement, the feature draws on information from several sources, including your purchase history, product reviews and items saved to Lists. Searches and conversations with Alexa for Shopping can also influence what Amazon learns. For example, someone who regularly buys dairy-free milk might receive recommendations for other dairy-free products. A shopper researching gardening supplies could start seeing suggestions for fertilizer or companion plants. That sounds useful enough. However, Amazon can also develop assumptions about your personal preferences from individual purchases or short-lived interests. That's where things can get awkward. Amazon's About You feature is already amusing shoppers Some shoppers have started sharing screenshots of their Amazon profiles on social media. The results range from remarkably accurate to unintentionally hilarious. One Threads user discovered that Amazon had included the description "flat buttocks" in her profile. "I stumbled upon a page of assumptions that Amazon has made about me based on my purchases and I'm literally speechless," she wrote. She even acknowledged that the assessment wasn't entirely wrong. Still, it's hard to imagine anyone asking an online retailer for that particular evaluation. Meanwhile, another shopper shared a profile describing an obsession with minimalist, one-bag travel and a preference for Anker charging products. The shopper confirmed that Amazon had accurately identified those interests. A different user discovered that Amazon had recorded a "one-time specialty cheese exploration." The response was simple: "guilty." Other shoppers have shared descriptions such as "has no friends" and "cannot keep real plants alive." One woman even reported that Amazon had described her as a "fifty-year-old man." These are the kinds of assumptions that can leave you wondering whether Amazon knows you at all. My own profile included some remarkably specific observations. Amazon said I "do not like scary movies," "value professional grade audio equipment," "prefer dark chocolate treats" and "enjoy swimming." It even noted my regular fresh flower purchases. But one entry really surprised me. Amazon claimed my mother had stayed at a hotel with another person, whom it identified by name, and had a negative experience. I certainly didn't expect to find that kind of information about a family member in my shopping profile. These examples show how an algorithm can turn shopping activity into surprisingly specific personal descriptions. Of course, Amazon's conclusions may be incomplete or inaccurate. Buying something for a friend, for example, doesn't necessarily mean you have any personal interest in that product. YOUR PHONE MAY REVEAL DOCTOR, CHURCH AND PHARMACY VISITS Why Amazon knows so much about your shopping habits Every time you interact with Amazon, you potentially give the company another clue about your preferences. A product search can suggest an interest, while a purchase provides a stronger signal about something you wanted at that moment. Amazon also uses information from its AI shopping assistant. If you tell Alexa for Shopping that your cat prefers a particular flavor of food, Amazon can use that detail to recommend similar products later. According to the company, these interactions help make recommendations more relevant. However, a single purchase might reflect a temporary need rather than a lasting preference. Think about buying an unusual gift for a relative. You might suddenly find Amazon treating that purchase as evidence of a personal hobby. That raises another concern. Some purchases can indicate sensitive interests involving health, relationships or other aspects of your private life. Even when Amazon draws an incorrect conclusion, you may still want to remove it from your shopping profile. How to see what Amazon knows about you Amazon makes About You available through its Shopping app, mobile website and desktop website. You can review the information the company has associated with your profile and make changes. On the Amazon Shopping app or mobile website If you don't see About You using those steps, try this alternate route in the Amazon Shopping app: On Amazon's desktop website How to remove personal information from Amazon About You Here's where I would spend a few minutes if you use Amazon regularly. The company says About You lets you correct preferences, provide feedback and remove information you don't want used for personalization. Review and delete unwanted preferences If you want to correct a detail instead of removing it, open the entry and look for an edit or feedback option. Make your changes and follow the prompts to save them. Amazon hasn't established that every account will show identical editing controls. The available options may depend on the information displayed. Removing a detail from About You changes how Amazon uses that preference for personalization. It does not necessarily erase the original purchase, search or conversation from every Amazon system. How to reduce what Amazon uses for recommendations Editing your About You profile is a useful starting point. However, you should also review the activity that influences Amazon's suggestions. Remove items from your Amazon browsing history Amazon provides browsing history controls that can help reduce recommendations based on products you've viewed. Removing a product from the browsing history display should not be treated as confirmation that Amazon has deleted every record of the interaction. Adjust Amazon's shopping recommendations Amazon also provides controls for managing recommendations associated with past purchases. This can be particularly helpful when you've purchased gifts or products that have nothing to do with your interests. Review Alexa shopping interactions If you regularly use Alexa for Shopping, consider what you share during those conversations. Amazon says the assistant can remember details you provide and use them to improve future shopping experiences. Ask "What do you know about me?" to review the preferences Alexa can describe. Then use About You to correct or remove unwanted details. For additional privacy controls, review your Alexa privacy settings and voice history in the Alexa app or your Amazon account. Deleting voice recordings and removing shopping preferences are separate actions, so check both. Can you completely delete your Amazon shopping profile? Amazon provides ways to edit preferences and manage certain recommendation signals. However, the company hasn't established that removing everything displayed in About You permanently deletes all underlying information. Your purchase history, for example, can remain associated with your account even after you exclude an item from recommendations. Amazon may retain certain transaction records for operational or legal reasons. Also, About You is only one part of Amazon's broader personalization system. Correcting an assumption doesn't necessarily stop Amazon from generating new recommendations based on future shopping activity. If privacy is your priority, review your browsing history, recommendation settings and Alexa privacy controls rather than relying exclusively on the new profile page. Kurt's key takeaways I've always found Amazon's recommendations fascinating, but seeing 81 personal details in my own profile was an eye-opener. Some were surprisingly accurate. Others, including information about my mother, left me wondering how Amazon reached those conclusions. I appreciate being able to review and remove these details, but I'd like more transparency about what happens to that information afterward. My advice? Take a few minutes to check your own Amazon About You profile. You might be surprised by what the company thinks it knows about you. Would you be comfortable with Amazon building a personality profile from everything you buy and search for, or has online shopping personalization gone too far? articles.body:
A conservative AI safety group is calling for the U.S. to implement tighter restrictions on advanced chip sales to China and limit the development of “vastly superhuman AI” as part of a new framework for AI policy.

Humans First, chaired by former Tea Party leader Amy Kremer, laid out what it described as an “America First” policy framework.

“AI will supercharge our nation’s economy, improve our quality of life, and ensure we dominate around the world,” the group wrote. “But policy must always be focused on helping hardworking Americans and putting Humans First.”

The group is arguing for stricter export controls on high-end chips and other AI technologies, mandatory testing of models for extreme risks, mandatory public reporting of major AI incidents, developer liability for “reckless design” and a “red line” on self-improving AI.

It also called for an end to any federal use of Flock cameras and warrantless searches of private data, in addition to urging a halt on H-1B visa approvals and opposing federal preemption of state AI laws.

Humans First, which was initially created to organize across party lines, shifted its focus to conservative activists in April when it tapped Kremer to serve as chair.

The group has been a vocal critic of the data center build-out in recent months, leading a day of nationwide demonstrations in July and staging a cross-country bus tour opposing AI infrastructure that wrapped up earlier this month.

The group’s AI framework stands in contrast to the more hands-off approach currently championed by President Trump, who has argued stricter regulations could hamper the U.S.’s ability to compete with China.

Trump gathered major AI leaders at the White House late last month, where they signed on to a series of voluntary commitments to place internal controls on their models and allow for external auditing.

articles.title: Musk settles election lottery lawsuits over $1 million voter giveaways
articles.summary: Tech mogul Elon Musk agreed to settle two lawsuits over his $1 million check handouts to battleground voters in the 2024 election, according to court filings published Thursday. The suits, filed in the Western District of Texas, accused the Tesla and SpaceX CEO of defrauding voters when his America PAC offered a $1 million giveaway…
articles.body:
Tech mogul Elon Musk agreed to settle two lawsuits over his $1 million check handouts to battleground voters in the 2024 election, according to court filings published Thursday.

The suits, filed in the Western District of Texas, accused the Tesla and SpaceX CEO of defrauding voters when his America PAC offered a $1 million giveaway to swing-state voters every day leading up to the 2024 general election.

Musk first made the pledge in October 2024 in Pennsylvania, and he eventually made similar promises in Michigan, Nevada, Arizona, Georgia, Wisconsin and North Carolina.

“The only thing we ask for the million dollars is that you be a spokesperson for the petition,” Musk told a recipient he handpicked from the audience at the time.

The lawsuits argued that voters were misled when they signed the petition and were told recipients would be chosen at “random” as in a lottery. Musk told a Philadelphia judge that winners were not chosen at random but chosen to be paid “spokespeople for the group.”

The tech mogul was ordered to testify under oath in June but had not yet testified before the settlements were reached. The details of the settlement were not included in public filings, and The Hill reached out to the plaintiffs’ and Musk’s legal teams for more information.

In Wisconsin, Musk made a different pledge for $1 million check handouts to voters during the state’s Supreme Court election last year.

Musk initially announced in March 2025 that he would speak in Wisconsin, with entrance limited to those who had voted in the state’s Supreme Court election. He said on the social platform X he would “personally hand over two checks for a million dollars each in appreciation for you taking the time to vote.”

About 12 hours later, his post was deleted and replaced with another , clarifying entrance was limited to those who signed the petition against “activist judges.” Musk said the money would be given to “spokesmen” for the petition, and he went to hand out two checks during a campaign rally in Wisconsin.

La Crosse County, Wis., District Attorney Tim Gruenke (D) announced in August his office declined to press charges over the handouts, arguing that in the end, “nobody was paid anything of value for voting or promising to vote.”

Despite Musk’s efforts, the conservative candidate he backed, Brad Schimel, lost to Democratic-backed Susan Crawford, keeping the high court’s liberal majority.

While Musk has not made similar pledges this election cycle, the SpaceX CEO is shaping up to be the largest known donor of the 2026 midterms for Republicans.

articles.title: Major US grocery chains hit by cybersecurity incident
articles.summary: Ahold Delhaize's cybersecurity incident knocked online ordering and digital coupons offline at Stop & Shop, Food Lion, Hannaford and Giant Food stores.
articles.body: You pull out your phone to check your grocery store's digital coupons or place an order for dinner. Suddenly, the app won't open. The website is unavailable, and the groceries you were counting on for tonight may never arrive. For anyone who depends on online grocery shopping, that's a frustrating problem. That's the situation shoppers encountered this week at several major U.S. supermarket chains. A cybersecurity incident at grocery giant Ahold Delhaize forced the company to take some systems offline. The disruption affected Stop & Shop, Food Lion, Hannaford and the Giant supermarket chains. The company says its physical stores have remained open, although customers have experienced interruptions to online services. There's another reason this story deserves attention. The same company suffered a major data breach in 2024 that exposed personal information belonging to more than 2.2 million people. So, as investigators work to understand the latest incident, shoppers have a reasonable question: Could their personal information be at risk again? CHICK-FIL-A DATA BREACH EXPOSES CUSTOMER ACCOUNTS Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Join us Saturday, October 31, at 11 AM ET / 8 AM PT. Register free now at CyberGuyLive.com. FRENCH SUPERMARKETS FACE MILLIONS IN LOSSES AFTER CYBERATTACK HITS REFRIGERATORS NATIONWIDE Major grocery cybersecurity incident affects five US supermarket chains On Oct. 12, Ahold Delhaize confirmed a cybersecurity issue within its network. The Netherlands-based company owns some of America's best-known regional supermarket chains and operates more than 9,400 stores worldwide. The company took certain systems offline to protect its operations while security teams investigated the problem. In its official statement, Ahold Delhaize said: "Our teams are taking steps to assess and mitigate the issue. This includes taking some systems offline to help protect them." The company serves approximately 60 million customers each week across its international businesses. Consequently, a problem involving its technology can affect grocery shopping far beyond a single store. Which US grocery stores are affected? The cybersecurity incident has disrupted online services for five major U.S. supermarket chains: According to Grocery Dive, websites and mobile apps for all five chains were still unavailable on the morning of Wednesday, Oct. 14. That marked at least the third consecutive day of online disruptions. Customers have encountered problems accessing online ordering and digital coupons. Some app-based loyalty features have also been unavailable. In its Oct. 13 update, Ahold Delhaize said it was beginning a controlled relaunch of certain systems. However, as of Oct. 14, the company had not announced a firm timetable for restoring all affected services. Are Stop & Shop, Food Lion and Hannaford stores still open? Yes. In its Oct. 13 statement, Ahold Delhaize confirmed that its supermarkets across Europe and the United States remained open and were serving customers. Notices from the affected U.S. chains also indicated that pharmacies were operating during their normal business hours. However, online shopping has experienced significant disruptions. Customers have faced interruptions to grocery pickup and delivery services. Meanwhile, shoppers who rely on digital coupons have encountered problems accessing their usual discounts. As of Oct. 14, Food Lion, Giant Food and The Giant Company also directed customers to third-party delivery services, including Instacart, DoorDash and Uber Eats, where available. For customers who depend on grocery delivery because of mobility challenges or limited transportation, these disruptions can create a serious inconvenience. What happens to online grocery orders and refunds? If you placed an online grocery order that was never fulfilled, the affected supermarket chains said customers would receive refunds for those orders. However, it's worth checking your credit card or bank account to make sure the refund actually arrives. Keep your original order confirmation and any emails related to the purchase. If the refund doesn't appear within the retailer's stated processing period, contact customer service through a verified channel. If your grocery app remains unavailable, shopping inside a physical store may be your most dependable option. Still, consider calling ahead if you need a specific service or want to confirm that a prescription is ready. Grocery giant moves toward restoring systems after security incident On Oct. 13, Ahold Delhaize issued a statement, updated Oct. 14, saying it was in the process of starting a controlled relaunch of certain systems. The company said it was working with external cybersecurity experts and appropriate authorities to investigate the incident. In a direct response to CyberGuy, an Ahold Delhaize USA spokesperson provided an update on efforts to restore affected services. "Please know our teams are working as quickly as possible to restore systems safely that we took offline as a precautionary measure, including our websites," the spokesperson told CyberGuy. The spokesperson also confirmed that stores remain open and apologized for the disruption to customers. However, Ahold Delhaize has not publicly identified who caused the problem or explained how its network was compromised. It has also not confirmed whether ransomware played a role. That leaves several important questions unanswered, including how the incident began and when all affected services will be restored. The company has not provided a firm timetable for full restoration. Was customer data stolen in the grocery cybersecurity incident? This may be the biggest concern for shoppers who have online grocery accounts. In its statement, Ahold Delhaize said investigators had found no evidence at that point that customer, employee or partner data was taken during the incident. That's encouraging for shoppers who have provided personal information to these supermarket chains. However, investigators were still examining the incident as of that update. The company's preliminary findings do not definitively rule out data theft. As of Oct. 14, Ahold Delhaize had not confirmed that personal information was stolen during this latest incident. That means shoppers should remain alert without assuming their personal information has been compromised. Ahold Delhaize suffered a major data breach in 2024 Unfortunately, this isn't the first major cybersecurity incident involving Ahold Delhaize. In November 2024, hackers gained unauthorized access to internal U.S. business systems operated by Ahold Delhaize USA Services. The attackers obtained files containing sensitive personal information. The company eventually disclosed that more than 2.2 million people were affected. According to a filing with the Maine Attorney General, the breach involved approximately 2.24 million individuals. In a June 2025 breach notification, the company explained that the stolen information varied by person. Exposed records could include: The vast majority of those affected were current or former employees, along with their dependents and beneficiaries. The company said it had no indication that customer payment or pharmacy systems were compromised during the 2024 attack. The ransomware group INC Ransom claimed responsibility for the earlier incident. However, Ahold Delhaize did not publicly confirm the group's involvement. There is currently no confirmed connection between that attack and the October 2026 cybersecurity incident. Why repeated cybersecurity incidents raise concerns For many of us, grocery shopping now involves much more than walking into a store with a shopping list. We create accounts, save payment details and use loyalty programs to access discounts. Some families depend on online ordering every week. When a supermarket chain experiences a cybersecurity incident, those conveniences can suddenly disappear. For Ahold Delhaize, the challenge now extends beyond restoring its apps. The company also faces questions about the security of its systems after experiencing two major incidents in less than two years. Customers deserve to understand what happened once investigators have reliable answers. 7 ways to protect yourself after a grocery store cybersecurity incident Even without confirmed customer data theft, a widely reported cybersecurity incident can give scammers opportunities to target shoppers. These seven precautions can help you protect your information and avoid additional headaches. 1. Watch for fake grocery refund messages Scammers may send emails or text messages claiming that you need to verify your payment information to receive a grocery refund. Those messages can seem especially convincing if you've recently had an order canceled. Avoid clicking unexpected refund links. Instead, review your original payment account or contact the retailer using a verified phone number. Never provide your banking password or pay a processing fee to receive a refund. 2. Review your grocery orders and charges If you placed an order around the time of the outage, check whether the store charged you for groceries you never received. Save your confirmation emails and keep any receipts. Then, review your account for a refund. If the money doesn't appear within the retailer's stated processing period, contact customer service or your payment provider. 3. Secure your grocery store account password If you reuse your grocery account password on other websites, replace it with a unique one. A password manager can generate and store strong passwords without forcing you to remember each one. Also, enable two-factor authentication (2FA) if your grocery account supports it. That gives your account another layer of protection against unauthorized access. 4. Be suspicious of unexpected security alerts A real cybersecurity incident gives scammers an opportunity to send convincing fake breach notifications. You might receive a message claiming that your grocery account has been compromised and that you must immediately verify your identity. Before entering personal information, confirm the alert through the retailer's official communications. 5. Monitor your financial accounts and personal information Although Ahold Delhaize reported no evidence of data theft in its Oct. 14 update, regularly checking your financial accounts remains a smart precaution. Enable transaction alerts through your bank or credit card provider. Pay attention to unfamiliar charges or unexpected account activity. 6. Check your digital coupons and loyalty discounts If you normally use your grocery store's app to access digital coupons or loyalty rewards, check your receipt carefully. Some discounts may be unavailable while the retailer's online services are down. Before checking out, ask a store employee whether there's another way to receive an advertised discount. Keep your receipt if you believe you were overcharged so you can request an adjustment when customer service becomes available. 7. Take action if you've clicked a suspicious link If you clicked a suspicious grocery refund or security alert link, your next steps depend on what information you shared. If you entered your password, change it immediately through the retailer's official website once it's available. Update any other accounts using that password. If you provided credit card or banking information, contact your financial institution and ask about securing your account. You can also report suspected fraud to the Federal Trade Commission at reportfraud.ftc.gov. If you downloaded a suspicious attachment, run a security scan using strong antivirus software on your device. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com. Kurt's key takeaways I find it troubling that a company responsible for feeding millions of American families is dealing with another major cybersecurity incident so soon after its last one. We depend on grocery stores for something as basic as putting dinner on the table. Increasingly, those stores also want us to use their apps to access the best prices and place orders. What concerns me is how quickly those everyday conveniences can disappear when something goes wrong with a retailer's technology. And after the 2024 breach exposed personal information belonging to more than 2.2 million people, I think Ahold Delhaize has some serious questions to answer. I'd like to know what caused this latest incident and whether the company addressed weaknesses identified after the previous attack. Those answers could go a long way toward restoring customer confidence. As of the company's October 14 update, investigators had found no evidence that customer, employee or partner data was taken in the latest incident. That's reassuring, although the investigation continues. In the meantime, you should remain cautious about unexpected refund messages or suspicious security alerts. If your grocery store suffered two major cybersecurity incidents in less than two years, would you still trust it with your personal information, or would you take your business somewhere else? articles.title: The US federal budget deficit for 2026 just came in. It's $1.992 trillion.
articles.summary: The US federal budget deficit for 2026 officially came in Friday at $1.992 trillion, a final tabulation to close out the government's fiscal year and another...
articles.body:
The US federal budget deficit for 2026 officially came in Friday at $1.992 trillion, a final tabulation to close out the government's fiscal year and another reminder of Washington's spiraling reliance on red ink.

This deficit number represents about 6% of the US gross domestic product and was a result of $5.403 trillion in total revenues for the fiscal year against total spending of $7.396 trillion.

The 2026 reading is a 12% jump from 2025's $1.775 trillion deficit.

These final numbers came in the Treasury Department's Monthly Statement for September, which covers the final month in the US government's fiscal calendar.

The red ink has led to dire warnings from economists that the US now routinely runs annual deficits that were previously seen only during recessions and wars. The gross US national debt passed $40 trillion in August and now sits above $40.3 trillion.

The latest "Debt to the Penny" reading from the Treasury Department came this past Wednesday, putting the gross US national debt at $40,329,229,827,541.02.

The independent budget hawks at the Committee for a Responsible Budget noted in a recent analysis that "the country's future fiscal outlook is even more dismal," noting that annual deficits could reach $3.1 trillion by 2036 without a change in the fiscal trajectory.

The group noted that annual interest costs on the debt are now $1.1 trillion, a record 3.4% of GDP, making it the second-largest line item in the government's budget. Interest on the debt still costs less than Social Security , but it is now more expensive than either Medicare or the defense budget.

Members of President Trump's team have tried to downplay this year's tabulation — the highest annual deficit reading other than 2020 and 2021, when budgets were inflated by COVID-era spending — as a blip and insist that the US fiscal situation is getting under control.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has focused on the Supreme Court-ordered tariff refunds that have turned a revenue stream into a cost center for the government in recent months.

Indeed, the impact of tariff refunds has been significant: $144.6 billion in tariff refunds were given out over the past year — but analyses of the deficit also show a variety of factors that have driven up deficits.

A Hamilton Project tracker of government expenditures shows how government spending has increased at a steady pace in 2026. The tracker looks at spending by calendar year and shows that as of Oct. 14, government spending has jumped each of the last three years.

articles.title: Oil hits $110 per barrel for first time since May
articles.summary: An international oil benchmark hit $110 per barrel on Friday, as the industry faces persistent shocks from the U.S.-Iran and Russia-Ukraine wars. The price of Brent crude oil, the international standard, hit $110 on the nose during Friday trading. That marked the first time it has reached that level since May 20, less than three…
articles.body:
An international oil benchmark hit $110 per barrel on Friday, as the industry faces persistent shocks from the U.S.-Iran and Russia-Ukraine wars.

The price of Brent crude oil , the international standard, hit $110 on the nose during Friday trading. That marked the first time it has reached that level since May 20, less than three months after the U.S. and Israel launched the Iran conflict.

The commodity is trading at roughly $109.75 as of late Friday afternoon.

Brent crude prices peaked in late April, when the benchmark topped $120 per barrel.

Oil prices shot up during the early months of the conflict with Iran and sunk down below $80 per barrel throughout much of June and July — as the U.S. and Iran were operating under a ceasefire both sides accused the other of violating.

But as the war, now approaching the eight-month mark, has persisted, oil prices have surpassed $100 yet again.

West Texas Intermediate crude, the North American benchmark, also topped $100 per barrel on Friday for the first time since Sep. 21.

The increase in oil prices has translated to higher prices at the pump for Americans. Regular gas in the U.S. costs about $4.33 per gallon on average, AAA reported Friday.

Diesel also costs more than $6.30 on average, nearly $2.70 higher than a year ago, according to AAA.

“Americans have now spent $135 billion more on gasoline and diesel purchases since March 1 than the same period last year,” Patrick De Haan, the head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, wrote Friday on the social platform X.

President Trump has sought to address rising costs, including via a deal with Russia for that country to boost its supply of diesel fuel to the global marketplace.

Ukrainian forces have launched strikes at Russian refineries amid the two countries’ ongoing war, as the two countries defy Trump’s proposed energy ceasefire .

articles.title: US measles cases top 4,400, far exceeding last year’s totals
articles.summary: National measles cases this year have now exceeded 4,400, all but guaranteeing the country will more than double the number of measles infections confirmed last year, which totaled 2,289. The latest update from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) on Friday recorded 4,410 total cases in 2026 just a week after the U.S.…
articles.body:
National measles cases this year have now exceeded 4,400, all but guaranteeing the country will more than double the number of measles infections confirmed last year, which totaled 2,289.

The latest update from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) on Friday recorded 4,410 total cases in 2026 just a week after the U.S. surpassed 4,000 cases .

When pressed for answers on the worsening situation on Thursday, before the new numbers were released, Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. placed blame on Dr. Anthony Fauci, a longtime National Institutes of Health scientist.

“We’ve done better than — we’re having a global measles outbreak right now,” Kennedy said when he was asked by a reporter about the six probable measles deaths that have been confirmed so far this year.

“It’s all over the world. The measles outbreak is occurring because so many people went unvaccinated during the COVID pandemic. And this is something that Anthony Fauci, in fact, predicted,” Kennedy said.

Kennedy was referring to Fauci’s private diary entries that were publicized by Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) earlier this year.

In an entry dated May 6, 2020, Fauci wrote, “Had conversation with Bob Redfield last night about the fact that >1 million children world-wide have missed their measles vaccinations because of the shutdown. This is terrible and needs to be addressed since on that basis alone, there would be far, far more excess deaths from measles among children than coronavirus deaths among children.”

U.S. measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccination rate among kindergarteners have been falling away from the ideal 95 percent coverage for several years now. This vaccination rate is considered necessary to stop widespread outbreaks.

During the 2025-26 school year, the CDC reported an MMR coverage rate of 92.4 percent. While still high, that figure represents hundreds of thousands of kindergarteners attending school while vulnerable to measles.

“We have done better and particularly my administration has done better at controlling the outbreak than any other country in the world,” Kennedy continued, arguing Canada and Mexico are experiencing worse outbreaks than the U.S.

Kennedy was commenting at an event with Rep. Jen Kiggans (R-Va.). A staffer attempted to bar the question about measles, before the reporter said Kennedy is the “highest ranking health official in the country. He can answer that question. He’s a Cabinet secretary.”

The U.S. and Mexico are scheduled to meet with the Pan American Health Organization next month to go over their respective measles elimination statuses.

Kennedy has softly endorsed the MMR vaccine, calling it the most effective way of stopping measles spread last year and in August said parents should get their children vaccinated against the virus. At the same time, however, he has continued to cast doubt on the safety of childhood vaccines.

During a September conference hosted by Children’s Health Defense, the anti-vaccine group he previously chaired, Kennedy claimed “vaccine-injured children” were “damaged” by conditions like asthma and autism and said sudden infant death syndrome and anorexia were common side effects.

The CDC vaccine advisory panel that Kennedy restaffed with ideological allies voted this year in favor of reducing the number of recommended childhood vaccines, though a federal judge disbanded the committee and blocked its votes. Earlier this month, the HHS launched a new clinic dedicated to vaccine-related injuries.

articles.body:
Centcom commander says naval blockade cost Iran $25B in oil revenue

The U.S. Central Command (Centcom) Commander Adm. Brad Cooper said on Friday that the U.S. naval blockade has cost Iran $25 billion in crude oil export revenue.

“As a point of emphasis, with the exception of the humanitarian assistance we’ve allowed in, Iran has no exports and no imports by sea,” Cooper said in a video. “The sum total of these actions has imposed devastating costs on Iran’s security apparatus and the IRGC specifically.”

Centcom forces have been readying for a possible restart of major combat operations versus Iran while the U.S. has continued to inflict economic pain on the Islamic Republic with sanctions and the naval blockade.

“The financial strain on Iran’s military has become so significant that there are reports of Iran-aligned militia groups across the region withholding payments to their soldiers in order to funnel money back to the IRGC , which also is not paying its troops,” he said.
